Rick Sanchez is a poor, battered, traumatized former little boy who had every bit of softness viciously abraded away and has spent decades welding armor directly onto his soul, and he’s agonizingly caught between wanting to save his grandson from experiencing that same pain and wanting him to just fucking get it over with. He lacks the strength and introspective capacity to even acknowledge the fact that he’s struggling with this dilemma—

(Because caring is something he supposes he is not supposed to do, because caring is a vector by which more pain happens)

—and so he just fumbles his way forward, half-conscious and incoherent, in haphazard and self-sabotaging dialogue with his own envy and loss and regret, motivated just as much by [infantile tantrums] and [a total lack of self-control and perspective] as he is by [a genuine desire for Morty’s well-being]. He has reasons for being strategically cruel to Morty, and he has reasons for being protective, and he’s also just a broken and randomly abusive patriarch, it’s not like he’s doing any of this in anything like a consistent or principled manner, it’s all an absolute mess of overkill and overcorrection and post-hoc rationalization intermixed with searing moments of unbearable shame and self-awareness and the whole thing rings incredibly true to my sense of what “parenting” actually looks like, out there among the humans.

(It feels more honest than most depictions. Less whitewashed and anesthetized, less neatly organized. I’m so used to a show having either Good Parents or Bad Parents that it’s mesmerizing to see something that feels Real.)

And I can’t look away. It’s an exquisitely heartbreaking study of the evolution of a soul, toward someone who will either end up viewing the game of Truth or Dare as an opportunity for fun and vulnerability and novelty and connection and the thrill of unscripted possibility…

…or as a lame and meaningless pantomime for babies whose existence doesn’t matter and contains nothing of value or interest in the first place.

(The divide between Rick and Morty is not the same as the divide between the people who thought my truths and dares were awesome and those who thought they were dangerous. But it’s the same kind of divide. It’s a gulf of worldviews, filters, incompatible-yet-equally-coherent perspectives.)

The kicker is, Rick knows—from his own sad experience—that the parts you cauterize don’t just grow back. That the process of endarkening the soul is (mostly) a one-way ratchet. Rick knows (because he’s caught in them himself) that cynicism and nihilism are memetic traps—that once you lose your grip on the thread of meaning, it’s incredibly hard to find it again. Most of Rick desperately wants Morty to wake up to the fact that none of this matters and there’s no point to any of it (mainly so he’ll stop being so god damn annoying all of the time).

But he’s also acutely aware that, once that critical step is taken, there’s nothing left to do but kill time until the clock runs out.

And because Rick and Morty doesn’t pull its punches, what we get in response to this fundamental question is … both. Neither. Unpredictable whiplash, unrelenting ambiguity. Rick’s unstrategic flailing, and the show’s ongoing and absolute refusal to provide anything like closure or resolution or relief.

(Awfully familiar, isn’t it? Wubba lubba dub dub.)

Scene II: The problem with Rhonda Byrne’s 2006 bestseller The Secret

I’ll be honest: I haven’t read The Secret.

For the purposes of this essay, I think that doesn’t matter. The impact that it had on my society wasn’t about the specific words that Rhonda Byrne wrote down—it was about what people thought the book said, what they told each other it said, the actions that they took in the wake of its passing.

My society believed that The Secret was about an only-slightly-more-woo version of the mechanism I laid out in the interlude above—namely, that people elicit the universe’s treatment of them, via their vibes and their beliefs and their behavior.

According to (my society’s understanding of) The Secret, bad things happen to people who summon badness from the ether. If you want good things to happen instead, the thing you had to do was manifest that goodness. To think positively, visualize success, emit the energy you wanted the universe to reflect back at you.

Ultimately, the recommendation of this essay will be something like “yes, that, but not in a stupid, destructive, and counterproductive way.” I think that The Secret (or at least, what the people around me seemed to be taking away from it circa 2006) was stupid, destructive, and counterproductive, and I want to briefly pause to point at why.

— Item 1: Victim blaming.

“Ah, bad things keep happening to you, even though you swear you’re manifesting as hard as you can, eh? Must be a skill issue.”

— Item 2: Epistemic virtue.

“What do you mean, you’re having a hard time ‘believing’ that good things are coming your way, given that you’ve experienced decades of unrelenting hardship and loss and failure and disappointment? Just … you know, override.”


(I did say it would be brief.)

The straw version of The Secret that ended up in the zeitgeist (regardless of whether the actual book said something saner) failed to take the problem seriously. The common narrative at the time was look, here’s this One Weird Trick that Just Works—

(And unfortunately, among the thousands and thousands of people who tried there were enough random success stories that that very narrative was compelling to people who were already doing the confirmation bias thing by default.)

—which meant that enacting the strategy espoused by The Secret allowed a tiny, lucky fraction to escape, encouraged a bunch of broken, twisted thinking all around, and gave the majority of sufferers yet another reason to believe that the world hated them and nothing would work and everything was going to be terrible forever (and also did you know it’s your own fault and you asked for it?).

The part The Secret overlooked is, people who are stuck in the dark world believe the things that they believe for reasons. There’s momentum and inertia behind their problems, evidence underpinning their worldview. It is not crazy for someone who’s been raped by six different partners to believe that their seventh partner might rape them, and it is a bad idea (and honestly more than a little bit cruel) to suggest that such a person “manifest positivity” rather than, say, keeping an eye out for red flags.

I’m going to borrow some words from CJtheX’s Bo Burnham vs. Jeff Bezos; here, CJ is talking about the algorithms behind sites like Amazon and Facebook and Youtube rather than social and psychological traps, but the basic complaint is the same and applies equally well:

We don’t let children vote until they’re 18, because we don’t think that they’re mature enough to understand the consequences of their actions. So why in God’s desecrated hell would they be good at voting with their baby attention spans against the megacorporation using casino techniques on their minds??

For that matter, why do we expect any individual to win this psychological war against the most overwhelmingly powerful institutions in history? That’s the problem with individualism—it’s always preached by people for whom individualism worked.

Good for you—you’ve done the best you can with what you’ve been given. Holy shit, look at all your agency! I’m happy you’ve taken control of your own life through your own actions. For real! Good for you! I’m happy you overcame adversity! But the system is still having its way with everybody else.

Why in God’s desecrated hell would a person who’s been beaten down over and over again and driven into a sad, tortured, pessimistic corner of the world where in fact the vast majority of the people they encounter do not have their best interests at heart and most of the things they will try to improve their lot will not move the needle—

Why in God’s desecrated hell would we expect that such a person will be able to think positive with sufficient enthusiasm, dexterity, and stamina to singlehandedly unravel the web of misery that formed around them over the course of decades?

It works, but it’s not easy. There’s a huge gap between the concept of a marathon and the mental and physical fortitude required to run one.

Scene III: Escape velocity

Beth Thomas spent the first five or so years of her life experiencing extreme neglect and abuse. She was rescued from her father and placed into the care of adoptive parents, but her violent tendencies and flat statements that she would kill them in their sleep if she could caused them to lock her in her room at night, deepening and furthering her alienation. At the age of six, she exhibited the full list of symptoms of psychopathy—lack of empathy, poor impulse control, active antipathy toward the people around her, etc.

Eventually, Beth came under the care of Dr. Ken Magid, a clinical psychologist who began controversial treatment program that involved intensive behavior modification, including a sort of fake-it-’til-you-make-it regimen of mimicking the surface appearance of empathy.

Over the course of literal years, the combination of [teaching Beth the external behavioral patterns of a person with healthy emotional attachments] and [making sure to provide her brain with no further training data on patterns of abuse] began to work. Slowly, Beth’s brain started to unlearn the self-protective patterns of psychopathy, and form new grooves around the experience of safety and abundance and secure attachment.

Eventually, Beth recovered from psychopathy, her brain gaining the ability to spontaneously generate emotions like remorse, which standard wisdom held was infinitely beyond the reach of therapeutic medicine.

(To be fair, Beth had the advantage of youth and mental plasticity; it’s plausible (although not, in my opinion, obvious or certain) that adult psychopaths can’t be fully healed via a similar process.)

By adulthood, Beth was essentially normal—or at least, visibly indistinguishable from a normal person—and went on to live a productive, cooperative, social life, including becoming a nurse and working with other severely abused children. When her treatment team came under fire for some of the controversial things they had done, Beth herself vigorously defended them, crediting them with (essentially) saving her soul.

There’s an excerpt from the end notes of Frank Herbert’s Dune which I have cited many times, and which feels appropriate to cite again. Concretely, it’s about the work involved in transforming barren desert into a self-sustaining ecosystem. Pragmatically, it lives in my mind as a kind of parable about slow, stepwise change.

Downwind sides of old dunes provided the first plantation areas. The Fremen aimed first for a cycle of poverty grass with peatlike hair cilia, to intertwine, mat, and fix the dunes by depriving the wind of its big weapon: moveable grains of sand. The engineered grasses were planted first along the downwind (slipface) side of the chosen dunes that stood across the path of the prevailing westerly winds.

With the downward face anchored, the windward faces grew higher and higher and more grass was planted to keep pace. Giant sifs (long dunes with sinuous crests) of more than 1500 meters height were produced in this way, creating a wind break.

When the barrier dunes reached sufficient height, the windward faces were planted with tougher sword grasses. Then came deeper plantings—ephemerals (chenopods, pigweeds, and amaranth to begin), then scotch broom, low lupine, vine eucalyptus, dwarf tamarisk, shore pine—then the true desert growths: candelilla, saguaro, and barrel cactus. Where it would grow, they introduced camel sage, onion grass, gobi feather grass, wild alfalfa, burrow bush, sand verbena, evening primrose, incense bush, smoke tree, cresote bush.

They turned then to the necessary animal life—burrowing creatures to reopen the soil and aerate it: kit fox, kangaroo mouse, desert hare, sand terrapin…and the predators to keep them in check: desert hawk, dwarf owl, eagle and desert owl; and insects to fill the niches these couldn’t reach: scorpion, centipede, trapdoor spider, the biting wasp and the wormfly, and the desert bat to keep watch on those.

Now came the crucial test: date palms, cotton, melons, coffee, medicinals—more than 200 selected food plant types to test and adapt.

If you are literally terraforming a literal desert, you can’t just start off by planting oaks. At the start, what you have is dead sand—loose and infertile, with no nutrients and a tendency to blow around. Even with irrigation, fertilization, and constant care, only the very hardiest of plants can survive in soil that looks like this:

But if you grow enough of those plants, then—as they die and decompose—they slightly enrich the sand, eventually allowing for a new generation of marginally-less-hardy and marginally-more-complex plants to come in and do the same.

It takes time, and many successive generations, to slowly transform the soil and create the preconditions for each subsequent layer of complexity to be laid down. And at each step of the process, you’re faced with a different set of problems—it’s a dozen distinct bioengineering challenges chaining into each other, one after another.

In the book Dune, the desert Fremen stoically accepted that this project had a timeline of centuries. They embarked upon it anyway, knowing that even their great-grandchildren might not live to see its halfway mark.

Pulling someone out of the dark world isn’t quite that ambitious. But it’s the sort of project that is best approached with the same patience and humility. Someone who has learned, via ten thousand shards of experience, that all is cold and cruel and hopeless, needs ten thousand more shards of experience in the opposite direction just to get back to zero.

(Okay, that’s an overstatement; brains do in fact update a little faster than that. But the general principle holds—the old patterns are still there, they often decay very slowly, and they’re ready to spring back to full power on very little encouragement. Someone who’s been primed to believe that there’s always a betrayal eventually, somewhere, can lose years of progress in an instant, because that single instant can recontextualize everything in between right back into the same old explanatory buckets.)

Things like “trust” and “vulnerability” and “openness” and “optimism” are tiny, fragile seedlings, surrounded by hardy, hungry weeds. It takes (or at least can take) deep care and sustained attention to deliver the right kinds of training data to a traumatized mind, especially if the person you’re trying to help is still embedded in the environment where wariness and cynicism and pessimism are adaptive, self-protective tools. The process of emerging from the darkness happens an inch at a time.

And this already-Herculean task is only made harder by the fact that you can’t merely provide them with data consistent with the light world hypothesis. Remember the concept of a memetic trap—someone with shit-tinted lenses glued to their face will see everything as shitty. If you want someone from the dark world to e.g. believe that a game of Truth or Dare is safe, it’s not enough to merely make it safe, in truth. You have to go much, much farther than that—provide the person with data that loudly and inarguably contradicts the dark hypotheses, is visibly inconsistent with their anticipations of Doom.

(And you have to do this with the understanding that their own brain may be working actively against your shared project, out of (e.g.) a self-protective desire to Not Get Their Hopes Up Only To Have The Rug Pulled Out From Under Them Yet Again (or some other similar sad pattern).)

(I said all of that very fast, and as I skim back over it, the main piece that feels missing is “also, you cannot and should not do this to someone, Rick Sanchez-style.” The process of slowly and carefully easing someone out of the dark world pretty much always requires consent; I think Beth Thomas probably didn’t consent, but she was an elementary schooler surrounded by a dedicated team capable of controlling and curating her entire environment 24/7 for multiple years. Most rescue efforts will take place under a rather different set of constraints.)

In short: the biggest danger is people failing to take the problem seriously. Failing to recognize that sloppy, partial attempts are particularly harmful—that they very quickly teach people to categorize things like “hope” and “help” and “possible paths to success” as just yet another delivery mechanism for pain and disappointment. Part of being trapped in the dark world is (often) having an extremely limited budget for escape attempts, just as desert sand has very little capacity to sustain plant life (at first).

(There’s a part of me that wishes I could offer more specific advice on how to heal the hurt, but I think that’s not what I should spend my remaining words on. Every situation will be different and no single concrete suggestion will be universally useful. The main thing I want is for people to understand something like “right, I can’t just wish my way into this person seeing the world the way I do; they are where they are because of a body of experiences that I cannot erase from their past; I need to actually balance those experiences out, and help them build a new worldview that also contains and explains those past experiences.” You can’t just transplant a sequoia from your own mind-forest. You have to help them build an entire self-sustaining ecosystem, one step at a time.)

Act IV

Scene I: Boy, putting Zack Davis’s name in a header will probably have Effects, huh


Treating all of the essay thus far as prerequisite and context:

This is why you should not trust Zack Davis, when he tries to tell you what constitutes good conduct and productive discourse. Zack Davis does not understand how high-trust, high-cooperation dynamics work. He has never seen them. They are utterly outside of his experience and beyond his comprehension. What he knows how to do is keep his footing in a world of liars and thieves and pickpockets, and he does this with genuinely admirable skill and inexhaustible tenacity.

But (as far as I can tell, from many interactions across years) Zack Davis does not understand how advocating for and deploying those survival tactics (which are 100% appropriate for use in an adversarial memetic environment) utterly destroys the possibility of building something Better. Even if he wanted to hit the “cooperate” button—

(In contrast to his usual stance, which from my perspective is something like “look, if we all hit ‘defect’ together, in full foreknowledge, then we don’t have to extend trust in any direction and there’s no possibility of any unpleasant surprises and you can all stop grumping at me for repeatedly ‘defecting’ because we’ll all be cooperating on the meta level, it’s not like I didn’t warn you which button I was planning on pressing, I am in fact very consistent and conscientious.”)

—I don’t think he knows where it is, or how to press it.

(Here I’m talking about the literal actual Zack Davis, but I’m also using him as a stand-in for all the dark world denizens whose well-meaning advice fails to take into account the possibility of light.)

Scene II: Whence Wholesomeness?

By this point, we’re almost to the bottom of the vast pile of things I came here to say. There will be a little bit less of a wrap-up and restatement than I usually like, because there isn’t really a small set of things to summarize. This hasn’t been a lesson so much as a guided meander around a section of reality; the intended takeaway is

[gestures vaguely]

Like any good meander, though, I think it’s best if we end up pretty close to where we began, making it easy to hop in the car and head for the nearest restaurant. Accordingly: there was one bit of commentary on my original truth or dare post that felt interestingly off-to-one-side from everything else we’ve talked about, and I think it’s a good focal point for the final thousand-or-so words.

A friend writes:

I think I am missing some kind of understanding of “the wholesome version of truth or dare” that allows me to steer towards it, or try to maneuver a social situation towards it.

I think the thing that I'm missing is like, some flavor of “bonding through minor/safe vulnerable transgression,” but more importantly, something like being less afraid of certain kinds of vulnerability. But, I also sort of feel like I have real reasons to be afraid of that vulnerability.

And also, like, there's a bunch of ways I'm not afraid to be vulnerable, or maybe certain normally-vulnerable-classed things aren't vulnerable for me. And there's something like “actually be vulnerable tho” that I'm missing.

BUT, knowing that much still leaves me feeling sort of confused about it

To start things off:

I think “bonding through minor/safe vulnerable transgression” is a bit of a red herring. I think that it is an important piece in the Truth or Dare puzzle, but I think it’s more of an incidental side effect. When people target bonding (or transgression!) they’re sort of putting the cart before the horse. It’s like trying to raise your self-esteem directly, instead of doing things of value and letting your self-esteem shift in response.

To the extent that my own experiences give me the right to make authoritative statements:

One way to recognize that you’re Doing The Wholesome Version (or headed in that direction) is that you’ll start to see a lot of transgressions of the type described in Benign Boundary Violations, where you’re pushing past social fences without actually breaching anyone’s individual boundaries.

At its best, Truth or Dare is a container that allows people to unlock stuff that was locked up by past trauma, or kept off-limits by broad social strictures that can be temporarily loosened for local benefit. The idea is to create an “asymmetric weapon” that knocks down obstacles in the path of wanted (or at least non-harmful) experiences, while not dragging anyone backwards through a hedge.

There’s something in this that rhymes with everybody being drunk in common knowledge; a part of what the container of Truth or Dare is for is plausible deniability à la “oh man, we were all so drunk last night.”

“Remember when Parker used the toothpaste to draw a—”

“HEY, come on, that was a dare.”

A good dare opens doors that 1) your friends and companions maybe want opened, and 2) that won’t hurt them if wrongly opened.

Okay, but what if I’m wrong about what counts as ‘safe,’ or what sorts of ponds my friends secretly want to be pushed into?

There’s a skill, here. A skill of careful exploration, gradual escalation, staying closely in touch with people’s responses and how the collective vibe feels. That skill is itself complex and hard to describe, but one direction to lean in, as you practice, is “make sure you know who the challenge is ‘for.’” If it’s just for your own entertainment, or it’s on behalf of the group at the expense of the challenged, or it’s trying to cause some social effect outside of the scope of the game itself, 🚩.

Okay, but what if people are unskilled? What if I’m unskilled?

Valid concern! Part of the background is “sufficient buffer”/“sufficient money in the bank.” A sufficiently-high baseline of health and safety and feeling-good and being-happy-to-be-there, such that mistakes and missteps make people go “oof” instead of triggering meltdowns or breakdowns or panic attacks. It’s generally unwise to try to play Truth or Dare when you’re Elliott; it’s generally fine to play when you’re Alexis.

(Another way to think about this: Truth or Dare is not a game for moving people from the dark world to the light world; it’s a game for celebrating it once it’s already been achieved.)

Okay, but what about people with ill intent?

Um. What.

(The real answer, from the perspective of someone with light world privilege, is “wow, it did not even occur to me that you might be playing Truth or Dare with someone you think might have ill intent, because it did not occur to me that you might be hanging around someone with ill intent at all. Can you, um. Leave? Send them away? Not be spending time in the vicinity of known or suspected malefactors? Of course you shouldn’t play Truth or Dare with them, any more than you should expose your belly to them or give them your credit card number.”)

(The response, from the perspective of someone who lacks light world privilege, will unfortunately often be something like “no, I can’t. They’re my family/friends/roommates/romantic partners/colleagues/bosses/etc. I don’t have the luxury to not-be-around toxic or hostile people; if I got rid of all of them I would be completely alone and wouldn’t have a job and wouldn’t have a place to live.” Which is a) valid, b) sad, and c) yeah, more evidence that you shouldn’t be entering a container that only goes well if you can safely be vulnerable and have a solid resource buffer.)

To dig into “vulnerability” a little further:

There’s an activity that I used to help run, at CFAR workshops, called “Comfort Zone Exploration.” The idea was that people would briefly flirt with being-a-certain-way that was normally outside of their identity, in order to gather data on it and see whether perhaps the boundaries of their identity were drawn in suboptimal places.

(e.g. “try dancing, if you see yourself as not-a-dancer! Do some math, if you’re not a math person! Assert your social boundaries with much greater strength, or try not taking up so much space in the conversation, etc.”)

In three full years of working at CFAR and intermittently participating in the activity myself on a dozen different occasions, I managed to successfully do CoZE exactly once, and it wasn’t even at a workshop. It was at a multi-day BDSM camp in the woods that a friend I had a crush on tricked me into attending by first implying they were going and then refusing to let me back out of.

(“Refusing” is overselling it by an order of magnitude or more. I was besotted. Their face fell by a millimeter when I said I was thinking of skipping it, and that was enough.)

What happened was: I got up on stage in front of a bunch of strangers naked—

(This being a thing I’d done before, and knew I was comfortable with.)

—and I tried to sing the song The Bad Touch, by the Bloodhound Gang, into a karaoke microphone—

(This being a thing I’d done before, and knew I was comfortable with.)

—and wouldn’t you know, it turns out that two things that are each within your comfort zone can combine into one thing that’s way, way outside of it. I started physically sweating, somehow lost track of the words despite knowing the song by heart and having them scrolling across the screen in front of me, and found myself embarrassed’ly trailing off into awkward silence with something like a hundred people expectantly staring at my penis.

And for a second I started preparing myself to give up and break off entirely and leave the stage, and then some quiet part of my brain whispered you know, it’s actually okay to just … fuck this one up. Like, we don’t know any of these people and we’ll never see them again. And you already know what it feels like to give up. What you don’t know is what it’s like to flub your way through a whole song for multiple agonizing minutes. Wanna find out?

And it turned out that I did.

The difference between the experience I had over the subsequent three minutes and the weirdly empty and unchallenging experiences I’d had at CFAR workshops is that I went into CoZE at the workshops braced.

I was armored up. I adopted an attitude that went something like This is fine. This is fine. I am supposed to do this. I am being virtuous. I am participating in the context where failure and discomfort are expected and permitted and encouraged and I am supposed to Try Something New and it’s Okay If I Fail and I am Okay With Whatever Happens and basically I was anesthetizing myself to the entire experience.

CoZE (as it turns out) (as I discovered while naked on stage in front of a bunch of forest fetishists) goes better when paired with something like genuine surrender. The same sort of relaxed openness one experiences while enjoying a massage. If you’re clenching through it, you don’t actually experience what it’s actually like to stand in that place, outside of your comfort zone—instead, you experience what it’s like to sortie into enemy territory, which is a very different thing.

The parallel with how to do Truth or Dare well is clear, I hope. I don’t know how to reliably create that sort of relaxed openness, on purpose. It requires some sort of Actual Safety that seems complicated to arrange, especially if you don’t have a clear sense of where the danger might lie, for a given activity with a given group of people.

(Focusing seems likely to help, there).

But just knowing that it’s an ingredient at all is probably news to some.

The last relevant/adjacent thread I want to tug on is my model of banter. A game of Truth or Dare does not necessarily require banter in order to be good, but it needs to be … growing in the same soil in which banter could also thrive? … or something. The prerequisites of banter are also the prerequisites of Truth or Dare, and the benefits of Truth or Dare overlap with the benefits of banter.

So. A model:

Imagine you commit a faux pas. You fart while everyone is eating, or you make a joke that lands flat, or you step on the popular kid’s glasses.

There are sort of three broad ways that everyone present might respond. The first is “non-response.” People could (basically) ignore it. Gloss over it, stay quiet, make a brief, token acknowledgement.

The potential spiral here is anxiety. “Oh god, did they notice, do they hate me, are they all silently judging me, is this it, is it all over, was that the last straw, are they all just humoring me, tolerating me, putting up with me, do they actually pity me—”

When nobody says anything, it can land as “Oh, nobody cares, cool.” But it can also land as crickets and everyone refusing to look you in the eye. As silent, uninteractable-with rejection, a too-late-to-do-anything-about-it cold shoulder.

The second sort of response is something like reassurance. People could tell you that it’s fine, no worries, no big deal, these things happen.

Again, there’s a sort of healthy, non-spiraling reaction to this, which is to, y’know, be reassured. But again there’s a way this can go south, which is something like “wait, why are they all being so solicitous, is there a double meaning here, am I actually coming across as weak or fragile or in-need-of-coddling or something, why are they rushing to try to make me feel better, is this all a bunch of white lies—”

The third broad category of response is banter. Being mocked, teased, ragged, made fun of.

The spiraling response to banter is to take it at face value, and conclude “oh god they all hate me/think I’m stupid/are mocking me/find me despicable.” To take the mockery personally.

(Which, to be clear, is sometimes called-for—sometimes you really are actually being mocked, by people who are using the pretense of banter as an excuse.)

But there’s a good thing that happens, when banter is well-meant and manages to land right, which is a kind of deep and full reassurance that isn’t (in my experience) deliverable through any other channel.

See, banter does something like acknowledge and dismiss the cost, in the way that silence fails to acknowledge it and reassurance fails to dismiss it (by instead making a big deal out of it). If I fart while we’re eating and everyone hastens to assure me that it’s fine, there’s some part of me that goes wait, what? It kind of isn’t?

But if everybody goes “eeeewwwwwwwww!” and there’s warm, spontaneous laughter and then someone teases me about having eaten broccoli or whatever and then someone else makes a joke about rotting corpses and then the humor spotlight moves smoothly onto someone else—

In that dynamic, it’s inescapably clear that a) everyone saw it, b) everyone was aware of the cost, and c) nobody cared.

In conjunction with visible, visceral acceptance, the teasing creates a sensation of something like abundance. Bounty. Safety. “Your account with us is so far into the green that we’re sitting here ragging you over losing twenty points like it’s nothing, like we’re not even worried that you’ll be worried because it’s just super clear that this is Not A Big Deal.”

It’s a relief because it dissipates the faux pas. It’s like when a toddler falls on the playground and the parents don’t rush over full of concern and comfort, but instead signal “nothing to see, here.” The part of us that instinctively looks to Everyone Else for a cue as to how seriously to take this is soothed by banter in a way that often can’t be achieved via any other response.

This isn’t a map, or a recipe. I don’t think you can take the above and automatically have wonderful games of Truth or Dare forever.

But hopefully it’s at least a pointer toward the bright and shiny thing that I see, and experience, and try to share with others.

The truth part of Truth or Dare is about being seen, with all of your blemishes and imperfections. Being seen is scary. It is, in fact, dangerous. It comes with real risk—

—except where it doesn’t. Except where you are, in fact, actually welcomed, actually accepted, actually safe.

When you have ten thousand points in the bank, you can sort of tell yourself that you’re wealthy by gambling with fifty of them without a lot of anxiety or caution. There’s a move that’s sort of like … like … like taking off your makeup in front of your new partner for the first time, or bringing a newish friend over without cleaning up first or Planning An Activity. A sort of relaxing-into-authenticity, a taking-a-gamble-that-they’ll-find-the-real-you-acceptable.

When that gamble pays off, it tends to be way more nourishing than the shallow security you felt in knowing that you could twist yourself into a Likeable Shape. A good game of Truth or Dare lets people roll those dice—lets them lower the mask and find out what actually happens.

But it’s only a wise bet to make in the first place if you either a) strongly anticipate that it’s going to be fine and nobody’s going to suddenly turn on you, or b) don’t actually care what these people think (and therefore can’t take substantial damage even if things go south).

If there is something there that can hurt you, then of course you’re going to have your shields up, and of course you’re not going to be able to (metaphorically) relax into the massage.

If you do need their love, and are simultaneously not confident/secure in it, then of course the idea of exposing the messy, unvetted, uncurated parts of yourself is going to fill you with anxiety, and make the experience unpleasant.

(A little bit of spiciness along those lines can be a good thing. It makes the experience bright and alive, gives it the thrill of a wrestling match or a leap into water. Betting with quarters is more exciting than betting with scraps of paper. You’re not actually trusting if it’s entirely justified, just like you’re not being tolerant if the thing you’re tolerating is something that didn’t bother you in the first place. But you probably don’t want to be gambling with your entire month’s paycheck, either.)

As for the dare part of Truth or Dare, it’s a little bit about being seen, too. Letting people see you as you sing at the top of your lungs, or run streaking across the backyard, or blush and giggle as you make a prank call to your ex. Letting people see your nervousness, or your courage, or your steely resolve. Letting them witness your dexterity or your flexibility or your wit or your poise.

But the rest of it is about freedom. Wildness. The thrill of not quite knowing what will happen, the uncertainty about how it will all turn out. It’s about not being fully in control, and a little bit about experimenting with trust—with letting other people take the wheel. Letting the people around you push you outside of your usual boundaries, and finding out what it’s like on the other side of the fence. Doing things you otherwise wouldn’t do—doing things you otherwise wouldn’t even think to do.

There is—or at least can be—a sort of self-fulfilling prophecy of empowerment, there, a positive feedback loop of the sort that drives you further and further into the light world. You enter a game of Truth or Dare because you think it’s probably going to be okay, you’re pretty sure you can handle it, you don’t know what’s going to happen but you feel excitement, jitters, nervous anticipation—

—and then it goes well, it is fun, it does surprise you, and your guts learn that you like these people and they like you and trying something a teensy bit risky and crazy is great, actually, you all had fun pushing each other around on the teeter totter and now you’re basking in a slightly-drunk afterglow.

(Or it goes badly, but it goes absorbably badly, mundanely badly, you didn’t put yourself at such risk that you have a horrible time, you just get … the absence of a potential good, and that’s fine, you could do that a bunch of times before it starts to wear away at your soul.)

That’s what Truth or Dare is like, in the light world. That’s what it feels like—like it has the potential for wild upside, a mainline expectation of solid fun, and a floor not much lower than “meh.”

That’s a really good bet to take! I’d push that button a bunch of times!

But if it doesn’t feel like that, to you—if the ceiling feels low, the floor seems cracked, and the mainline expectation is discomfort, embarrassment, anxiety, pain—

Maybe just don’t? Don’t. It’s a shame it’s like that for you, there’s definitely something here that Could Be Better, but the way to fix it isn’t by plugging your ears and going lalalalala.

Regarding the "Every Good Therapist Already Implicitly Understands Everything I Have To Say, Here," part of the subtitle -- yeah? I think that is probably true. It was definitely woven into / corraborated by my training and clinical experience.

We were also taught, and I believe, that therapy is one of the best ways for clients from various Dark Worlds to form long, deep, stable relationships with their therapist -- who is, ideally, an inhabitant of the corresponding Light World.

When this happens and it works, it can be a powerful way for the client to get a lot of training data about what it is like to interact with someone who doesn't defect, who in fact cooperates even when the client defects, and maybe the client eventually becomes brave enough to venture cooperating in the therapist-client relationship and have that go well.

And then if the therapist is very good they can help the client find safe places to cooperate in their life outside of therapy.

Firstly, thank you for writing this, I very much enjoyed it.

This put into words a feeling I've been struggling with for a while. A few years ago, my wife and I hosted thanksgiving for my family. By offering money, she signaled (unintentionally, likely just trying to be nice) that our relationship was more of the "discrepancies must be immediately rectified" type. Contrast that with if she had instead, say, offered to bring a dessert. Despite being financially identical, it feels more like we're all contributing to the green, a no one's keeping score dynamic.
